claims.text: The relatively low hardness of nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi stems from a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure lacking significant secondary phases and interfaces.
The relatively low strength of nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi stems from a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure lacking significant secondary phases and interfaces.
The absence of secondary phases and interfaces permits comparatively unimpeded dislocation motion.
Easy dislocation motion promotes plasticity in nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Easy dislocation motion promotes machinability in nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi material is a single-phase homogeneous solid solution with uniform grain size and no significant precipitates or secondary phases.
Controlled thermal treatment can nucleate fine precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Controlled thermal treatment can refine the grains of CoCrFeNiTi.
Minor alloying adjustments can promote precipitation or grain refinement.
Fine precipitates act as dislocation-pinning obstacles.
Refined grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The as-cast homogeneous solid solution has minimal lattice distortion.
Introducing precipitates or refined grains will increase hardness by obstructing dislocation motion.
Introducing precipitates or refined grains will increase strength by obstructing dislocation motion.
Thermally treated CoCrFeNiTi containing precipitates or additional grain boundaries will have greater hardness than the as-cast solid-solution state.
Thermally treated CoCrFeNiTi containing precipitates or additional grain boundaries will have greater yield strength than the as-cast solid-solution state.
The proposed mechanism applies under room-temperature or quasi-static loading and may change at high temperature or for non-equimolar compositions.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits minor alloying adjustments, whereas the conditions require composition to remain fixed at equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.

The boundary says the hypothesis applies to a single solid-solution phase, but the treated comparison is intended to introduce precipitates or phase changes and therefore may no longer satisfy that structural boundary.
